nodes.ask: Brought in after a collapse. First moves?
options: Monitor, vitals, 12-lead ECG, glucose if it could be low, and the story
Vitals, a 12-lead ECG, a 48-hour Holter before discharge, and the story
Vitals, a 12-lead ECG, an urgent EEG, and the story of what happened
Vitals, a 12-lead ECG, a tilt-table test today, and the story
nodes.chainStep: Cardiac monitor and vitals; a 12-lead ECG for everyone; the account of before, during and after from the patient and any witnesses
nodes.why: Everyone with a suspected blackout gets vitals, a 12-lead ECG and an account, from the patient and any witnesses, of what happened before, during and after. Arrhythmia is the commonest cause of a falsely negative San Francisco rule, so monitoring is part of the assessment. A Holter never replaces the 12-lead, and for infrequent blackouts it is not usually offered unless the 12-lead shows a conduction abnormality; EEG is not a routine test for a blackout, and a tilt test is not a first-line investigation.

orders.dose: Everyone. A red flag if it shows a conduction abnormality (bundle branch block or any degree of heart block), a long or short QT, or any ST segment or T wave abnormality

Without automated interpretation, look for persistent bradycardia, any ventricular arrhythmia, QTc over 450 ms or under 350 ms, a Brugada pattern, pre-excitation, ventricular hypertrophy, abnormal T wave inversion, pathological Q waves, a sustained atrial arrhythmia, a paced rhythm
Pulse, respiratory rate, temperature; lying and standing blood pressure if clinically appropriate; the drug list, looking for culprits such as diuretics

nodes.note: Not in this version: under-16s, cardiac arrest, head injury from the collapse, intoxication, syncope with a reduced ejection fraction or other structural disease on the echo.

outcomes.if: Bradycardia with shock; high-grade AV block or a very slow rate, with low pressure or confusion
Ventricular tachycardia; sustained, on the monitor

orders.dose: Immediate synchronized cardioversion with haemodynamic instability; an unsynchronized shock if synchronization is not possible

outcomes.if: Shock without bradycardia or VT; still hypotensive after coming round
Neither; no VT, no bradycardia, no shock

nodes.ask: Bradycardia with shock after a collapse. Treatment?
options: IV atropine, then pacing if the rate and pressure do not respond
Watch on the monitor; pace only if the collapse recurs
A permanent pacemaker first, before any drug or temporary pacing
Wait for the potassium and digoxin level before treating
nodes.chainStep: IV chronotropic drug (atropine); temporary pacing if it fails, transcutaneous as the emergency bridge and transvenous when available; labs for a reversible cause
nodes.why: Temporary pacing is emergency treatment for a bradyarrhythmia causing syncope or hemodynamic compromise, once an IV chronotropic drug has been considered; atropine is named, in the guideline's acute MI section, for vagally mediated bradycardia and AV block. Transcutaneous pacing is fast and non-invasive but less stable and needs sedation, so it is for the emergency or when transvenous pacing is not available. Labs for a reversible cause go alongside, and a permanent pacemaker follows promptly once its criteria are met.

sources.where: 11.3 recommendations regarding temporary cardiac pacing and text; 8.1 text; 4.3.4

orders.dose: Dose not stated in the open sources read
orders.note: The US ACLS bradycardia algorithm (AHA, Circulation) is barred from AI use and the ERC 2021 copy was not reachable; the dose needs one of them.

orders.dose: Bradycardia that compromises the circulation and does not respond to IV chronotropic drugs; also the bridge when a permanent implant is not immediately available
When transvenous pacing is not possible or available; emergency use only, under close hemodynamic monitoring, with sedation
orders.note: ESC 2021 ranks transcutaneous pacing behind transvenous; the US algorithm uses it as the first pacing step after atropine. Pacing is never delayed for a drug that has failed.

orders.dose: Thyroid function, Lyme titer, digoxin level, potassium, calcium and pH when clinically suspected

nodes.summary: Sustained VT after a collapse: immediate synchronized cardioversion when unstable (unsynchronized if synchronization is not possible); if tolerated, continue in the palpitations pathway's wide-complex route.

nodes.ask: No VT, no bradycardia and no shock. Next?
options: The witnesses' account; glucose, hemoglobin and a pregnancy test where they fit
Carotid sinus massage at the bedside to look for a reflex cause
An epilepsy referral, since the limbs jerked during it
Admit for telemetry before taking the history
nodes.chainStep: Full account from the patient and witnesses; glucose if hypoglycemia is possible, hemoglobin if bleeding or anemia is, a pregnancy test in any woman who could be pregnant
nodes.why: The account decides whether this was a blackout at all; if that stays uncertain, assume it was until proven otherwise, and a cause that needs immediate action is treated first. Glucose is checked when hypoglycemia is possible and hemoglobin when bleeding or anemia is. A pregnancy test is worth offering even when symptoms are non-specific: fainting and collapse are presentations of ectopic pregnancy, as syncope is of PE. Brief jerking happens in ordinary faints and is not by itself epilepsy. Carotid sinus massage is a later test, done with ECG recording and resuscitation equipment at hand, and an uncomplicated faint needs no further immediate management.

nodes.label: History, glucose, hemoglobin and pregnancy test

outcomes.if: Not a blackout; a trip or fall, aware throughout
Hypoglycemia; low glucose in a person with diabetes

orders.dose: Dose for a non-seizing patient not in the open sources read; the seizure pathway's AES dose (thiamine 100 mg IV, then 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV, glucose under 60 mg/dL) is for a seizure

outcomes.if: Seizure features; a bitten tongue, head turning, prolonged jerking or confusion afterward

orders.dose: Within 2 weeks when features strongly suggest a seizure: a bitten tongue, head turning to one side, unusual posturing, prolonged limb jerking, confusion afterward, déjà vu or jamais vu
Routine awake EEG if an epileptic seizure is suspected, ideally within 72 hours, through the seizure workup; not a routine test for a blackout that is not a suspected seizure
Must not drive while waiting for the specialist assessment

outcomes.if: GI bleeding; melena or hematemesis, often a low hemoglobin
Pregnancy test positive; in a woman who fainted
New breathlessness; or hypoxia, a swollen leg, a recent operation
Chest pain with the collapse; or pain tearing through to the back
Sudden severe headache; at or just before the collapse
Syncope; a blackout with full recovery, none of the above

nodes.summary: No loss of consciousness: a fall, not a blackout. Assess and manage it as a fall; this pathway stops here.
Hypoglycemia explains the collapse: give glucose now and find out why (insulin with a missed meal here); the non-seizure dose is pending a source.

Features that strongly suggest an epileptic seizure, not syncope: continue in the seizure pathway. From this guideline: an epilepsy specialist within 2 weeks, an EEG through the seizure workup, and no driving while waiting.
Syncope with GI bleeding: continue in the GI bleed pathway, which starts with hemodynamics and resuscitation.
Positive pregnancy test after a faint: continue in the abdominal pain pathway, where a transvaginal ultrasound locates the pregnancy.
Syncope with new breathlessness: continue in the dyspnea pathway, where PE is weighed by clinical probability.
Syncope with chest pain or an ischemic ECG: continue in the chest pain pathway, which covers ACS and aortic dissection.
Collapse with a sudden severe headache: continue in the headache pathway, where subarachnoid hemorrhage is excluded.

Shock after a collapse, without bradycardia or VT, is not a faint that has recovered: resuscitate and find the source now. Back pain or a pulsatile mass continues in the abdominal pain pathway (ruptured AAA); melena or hematemesis in the GI bleed pathway; a positive pregnancy test in the abdominal pain pathway; hypoxia or new breathlessness in the dyspnea pathway.

nodes.ask: Syncope with full recovery, no other cause found yet. Next?
options: The ECG and a red-flag screen before any disposition
Discharge: full recovery and normal vitals now mean a benign cause
An exercise test now, before the ECG is reviewed
Admit only if the troponin is raised; otherwise home with GP follow-up
nodes.chainStep: Screen the ECG and the red flags (an abnormal ECG, heart failure, syncope on exertion, a family history of sudden death under 40 or an inherited heart condition, new breathlessness, a murmur; consider it over 65 without warning); any red flag means urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours
nodes.why: A blackout with complete recovery still needs the red-flag screen. Any of these means urgent cardiovascular assessment, reviewed by a specialist within 24 hours: an ECG abnormality, heart failure, a blackout during exertion, a family history of sudden death under 40 or an inherited heart condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a murmur; consider it for anyone over 65 who blacked out without warning. Troponin is not on that list. An exercise test is for syncope during exercise, and waits for imaging if aortic stenosis or HCM is possible.

orders.dose: US practice admits high-risk syncope for monitored evaluation; the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS criteria were not readable in an open copy

nodes.note: These red flags follow NICE CG109. The 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS syncope guideline, the usual US frame, was not reachable in an open copy, so its high-risk list is not checked here; palpitations just before the event and chest pain are not on NICE's list. Palpitations just before the event and a blackout while lying down are high-risk features in the usual US frame; no case uses them until a source is read.

outcomes.if: High-grade AV block; Mobitz II, infranodal 2:1, high-degree or complete heart block
Long QT, Brugada or pre-excitation; on the 12-lead ECG
Acute ischemia on the ECG; ST elevation or new ischemic changes
Exertion, murmur, failure or family history; syncope on exertion, a heart murmur, heart failure, or sudden death in a relative under 40
Other red flags only; another ECG abnormality such as bundle branch block, or over 65 with no warning
No red flags; normal ECG, none of the above

nodes.ask: Syncope with high-grade AV block; stable now, or paced. Next?
options: Look for a reversible cause; permanent pacemaker if there is none
Discharge with a 48-hour Holter monitor and a cardiology letter
Observe, and implant a pacemaker only if the syncope happens again
A tilt-table test first, to look for a reflex cause of the block
nodes.chainStep: Labs and the drug list for a reversible cause; permanent pacemaker for Mobitz II, infranodal 2:1, high-degree or complete AV block, promptly; cardiac imaging; temporary transvenous pacing as the bridge if needed
nodes.why: Pacing is indicated for third-degree, second-degree type 2, infranodal 2:1 or high-degree AV block whatever the symptoms, so there is no waiting for another event, and the implant should be prompt once the criteria are met. It is not recommended when the block has a transient cause that can be corrected and prevented, which is why the labs and the drug list come first when a cause is suspected. Ambulatory monitoring is for a suspected bradycardia, to link rhythm and symptoms; this one is documented.

sources.where: 5.2 recommendations for pacing for atrioventricular block; 4.3.1; 4.3.4; 11.3 text

orders.dose: Third-degree, second-degree type 2, infranodal 2:1 or high-degree AV block in sinus rhythm, irrespective of symptoms; implant promptly once the criteria are met

orders.item: Pacing for a correctable transient cause
orders.dose: Not recommended (Class III)
Thyroid function, Lyme titer, digoxin level, potassium, calcium and pH when a cause is suspected
For structural heart disease and left ventricular function in symptomatic bradycardia

nodes.summary: High-grade AV block with syncope: an IV chronotropic drug and temporary pacing for shock, a correctable cause excluded, then a permanent pacemaker without waiting for another event.

nodes.ask: Syncope with long QT, a Brugada pattern or pre-excitation. Next?
options: Cardiac monitoring now, with urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours
Home today with a routine outpatient cardiology referral letter
A 48-hour Holter at home first, then decide on the referral
A tilt-table test today to look for a reflex cause first
nodes.chainStep: Cardiac monitoring; urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours; no exertion and no driving until assessed
nodes.why: These are ECG red flags. Long QT and Brugada syndromes predispose to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death and can present with syncope, and pre-excitation is on the same list, so the referral is urgent, reviewed by a specialist within 24 hours. While waiting, the patient avoids exertion and does not drive. For a suspected arrhythmic cause, a tilt test is not a first-line test.

sources.where: 1.1.2.2; 1.1.2.3; 1.1.4.1; 1.1.4.2; 1.3.2.4; 1.5.4.3; Terms: Brugada syndrome, long QT syndromes

orders.dose: Red flag for referral: QTc over 450 ms on a manual read (short QT under 350 ms); not the diagnostic threshold for long QT syndrome
Remove the offending QT-prolonging drug; manage provoking conditions such as hypokalemia (repleting potassium to 4.5 to 5 mmol/L may be considered)
Abnormal ST elevation in V1 to V3
Drug, device and ablation decisions for these conditions are not in the open sources read
Avoid physical exertion if relevant; do not drive
Unstable: electrical cardioversion. Stable: IV ibutilide or IV procainamide. AV nodal blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone, digoxin, adenosine, beta blockers) are contraindicated

sources.where: WPW and preexcitation syndromes, recommendations 1, 3 and 4

nodes.summary: Long QT, Brugada pattern or pre-excitation with syncope: urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours, monitored meanwhile, with no exertion or driving until assessed; the specific treatment is a specialist decision not covered here.

nodes.ask: Syncope with exertion, a murmur, heart failure or a family history of sudden death. Next?
options: Echo and cardiac monitoring, with urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours
An exercise test first, to reproduce the blackout safely
Discharge today with an outpatient echo in six weeks
A 24-hour Holter instead of any cardiac imaging
nodes.chainStep: Echo and urgent cardiology assessment within 24 hours; no exercise testing before imaging when aortic stenosis or HCM is possible; no exercise until assessed
nodes.why: Suspected structural heart disease is investigated with cardiac imaging, and these red flags make the assessment urgent, reviewed within 24 hours. Syncope during exercise does earn an exercise test, but not before imaging when aortic stenosis or HCM is possible, and until then the patient refrains from exercise. Arrhythmia stays possible in structural disease, so an ambulatory ECG may follow.

orders.dose: Refrain until told otherwise after the specialist assessment
Within 7 days for syncope during exercise, unless aortic stenosis or HCM needs imaging first

nodes.note: NICE NG208 sets urgent specialist assessment with an echo within 2 weeks for a systolic murmur with exertional syncope; NICE CG109 wants a blackout with a red flag reviewed within 24 hours. This route follows CG109.

outcomes.if: Severe aortic stenosis; on the echo
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; asymmetric septal hypertrophy with an outflow gradient
Structurally normal heart; no AS or HCM

nodes.ask: Syncope on exertion with severe aortic stenosis. Management?
options: Aortic valve replacement, surgical or transcatheter
Review with an echo every 6 to 12 months
An exercise test to confirm the symptoms
Medical therapy until symptoms limit daily life
nodes.chainStep: Refer for aortic valve replacement, surgical or TAVI by surgical risk; no exercise test; no exercise until reassessed
nodes.why: Symptomatic severe valve disease is an indication for intervention, and syncope on exertion is a symptom; there is no waiting for symptoms to worsen. Echo review every 6 to 12 months is for asymptomatic severe disease, and exercise testing unmasks symptoms in asymptomatic aortic stenosis rather than confirming them after a faint. NICE offers surgery first at low or intermediate surgical risk and TAVI, for non-bicuspid valves, at high risk or when surgery is unsuitable.

orders.dose: Surgical replacement first line at low or intermediate surgical risk; TAVI for non-bicuspid severe aortic stenosis at high surgical risk or when surgery is unsuitable
orders.note: NICE's choice rests partly on the UK list price of TAVI; the 2020 ACC/AHA valve guideline (JACC copy) was not reachable to compare.

orders.dose: Refrain until told otherwise after the specialist assessment

nodes.summary: Exertional syncope from severe aortic stenosis: a symptom of severe valve disease, so valve replacement, surgical or transcatheter; no exercise test and no exercise meanwhile.

nodes.ask: Syncope on exertion; HCM with an outflow gradient. Next?
options: Beta blocker, no vasodilators or diuretics, rest from exercise, risk review
A vasodilator to lower the afterload, then home with cardiology follow-up
Furosemide to offload the thickened ventricle, with a beta blocker
A beta blocker, and back to sport once the heart rate settles
nodes.chainStep: Beta blocker (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker if not tolerated or not effective); avoid vasodilators, diuretics and hypovolemia; no exercise until assessed; sudden death risk review for an ICD; echo for first-degree relatives
nodes.why: Beta blockers are recommended for symptoms in obstructive and non-obstructive HCM, with a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker when they fail or are not tolerated. Vasodilators should be avoided, especially with obstruction, and syncope in HCM can be triggered by hypovolemia, diuretics or vasodilators. Exercise waits for the specialist assessment. Unexplained syncope, not from obstruction or a vasovagal reflex, is a sudden death risk factor that weighs toward an ICD, and exertional syncope from a gradient over 50 mm Hg despite optimal medical therapy calls for septal reduction.

sources.where: Table 12; 2.7; SCD risk and ICD recommendations; septal reduction recommendations

orders.dose: Recommended for symptoms; the source names no agent or dose

If beta blockers are not tolerated or not effective. Verapamil: initial dose 40 mg three times a day, up to a maximum of 480 mg per day; strict monitoring with severe obstruction (100 mm Hg or more) or a raised pulmonary artery systolic pressure
Avoid, especially with outflow obstruction
Hypovolemia, diuretics, vasodilators and severe anemia can each trigger syncope in HCM
Consider at 40 or younger with one risk factor such as unexplained syncope (not from obstruction or a vasovagal reflex); over 40 to 60 by shared decision

sources.where: SCD risk and ICD recommendations, Class IIa

orders.dose: Exertional syncope from a resting or provoked outflow gradient over 50 mm Hg despite optimal medical therapy
Echo for first-degree relatives as initial family screening
Refrain until told otherwise after the specialist assessment

nodes.note: These recommendations come from the 2024 Brazilian Society of Cardiology HCM guideline, the open full text found; the 2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline (JACC copy) was not reachable to compare.

nodes.summary: HCM with exertional syncope: beta blocker, no vasodilators or diuretics, no exercise until assessed, sudden death risk reviewed for an ICD, septal reduction if a large gradient keeps causing syncope on full therapy, and echo for first-degree relatives.

nodes.ask: Red flags point to an arrhythmia; no diagnosis yet. Next?
options: Monitor now, urgent specialist review, then an ambulatory ECG by frequency
Home today with a tilt-table test booked before any ambulatory ECG
Home today with a 24-hour Holter
An EEG and a neurology referral to look for epilepsy
nodes.chainStep: Cardiac monitoring; urgent specialist review within 24 hours; ambulatory ECG by frequency (Holter if several a week, external event recorder every 1 to 2 weeks, implantable recorder if rarer); carotid sinus massage at 60 or older; no driving while waiting
nodes.why: A suspected arrhythmic cause gets an ambulatory ECG chosen by how often the blackouts come: a Holter for several a week, an external event recorder for every 1 to 2 weeks, an implantable recorder when rarer. When blackouts come less than once every 2 weeks, a Holter is not usually offered unless the 12-lead shows a conduction abnormality; a tilt test is not first-line here, and EEG has no routine place. Arrhythmia is the commonest cause of a falsely reassuring San Francisco rule, which is why monitoring is part of the assessment.

orders.dose: Several blackouts a week: Holter up to 48 hours; every 1 to 2 weeks: external event recorder; less often than every 2 weeks: implantable event recorder
24-hour Holter or in-hospital telemetry; events under once a month: implantable loop recorder
Electrophysiology study if still unexplained after non-invasive tests or when a pacing decision is urgent, unless empirical pacing is preferred, especially in the elderly and frail
First-line test for unexplained syncope at 60 or older, with ECG recording and resuscitation equipment; not after a TIA or stroke or with known carotid stenosis

sources.where: Recommendations for non-invasive evaluation, footnote c

orders.dose: Must not drive while waiting for the specialist assessment

nodes.summary: Red flags without a diagnosis: urgent specialist assessment, cardiac monitoring, then an ambulatory ECG chosen by how often the events come; no driving while waiting.

nodes.ask: Syncope, normal ECG, no red flags. Next?
options: Lying and standing pressure, and the history of posture, trigger and warning
Admit for telemetry and an echo before any discharge decision
An EEG, in case the blackout was really a seizure
A tilt-table test now, before any decision about discharge
nodes.chainStep: Lying, then standing blood pressure at 1 and 3 minutes; the history of posture, provoking trigger and warning symptoms; a validated risk score alongside judgment if the cause is unclear
nodes.why: With no red flags, the history and the standing pressure sort it: a posture such as prolonged standing, a provoking trigger such as pain or a procedure, and warning symptoms such as sweating point to an uncomplicated faint; a fall of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 diastolic after at least 1 minute standing confirms postural hypotension. An uncomplicated faint needs no admission or tilt test, and EEG is not routine. Risk scores can help when the cause is unclear, but most have low-quality evidence for routine use, and the Canadian score and the San Francisco rule overlap in performance.

orders.dose: Lying (or seated), then again after standing at least 1 minute; positive if systolic falls 20 mm Hg or more or diastolic 10 or more

Vasovagal predisposition (warm crowded place, prolonged standing, fear, emotion or pain) -1; heart disease +1; any ED systolic under 90 or over 180 +2; troponin above the 99th percentile +2 (not done scores 0); abnormal QRS axis (under -30 or over 100 degrees) +1; QRS over 130 ms +1; QTc over 480 ms +2; ED diagnosis vasovagal -2, cardiac +2, neither 0. Range -3 to 11: -2 or lower very low risk (under 1%), -1 to 3 low to medium (1 to 8%), 4 or more high (over 12%)

sources.where: Abstract; Table 4 and footnotes; Results; Interpretation

orders.note: The derivation paper gives the abnormal QRS axis as over 100 degrees in its abstract and over 110 in its Table 4. WJEM 2025 Table 1 prints QTc over 480 ms as +1, which cannot reach the -3 to 11 range stated by the derivation, the 2026 validation and WJEM's own introduction; +2 is used here. The low-risk cut is under 0 in the 2026 US validation and under 1 in the 2025 US study.

orders.dose: High risk with congestive heart failure, hematocrit under 30%, an abnormal ECG or monitor (new changes or non-sinus rhythm), shortness of breath, or a triage systolic under 90 mm Hg. Only when no cause is evident after the ED evaluation; a negative rule leaves 5% or lower risk of a serious outcome in all comers, and 2% or lower when applied only after no cause is evident
Most syncope decision rules have low-quality evidence for routine use; in a 2026 US cohort, physician-estimated risk did not differ from the CSRS

outcomes.if: Uncomplicated faint; posture, a trigger and warning, or micturition, cough or swallowing
Postural hypotension; systolic falls 20 or more, or diastolic 10 or more, on standing
Unexplained; no typical posture, trigger or warning, standing pressure normal

nodes.ask: Uncomplicated faint or situational syncope, no red flags. Next?
options: Home with reassurance, salt and fluids, and counter-pressure maneuvers
Admit for telemetry and an echo to exclude a cardiac cause
A tilt-table test before discharge to confirm the diagnosis
Home on fludrocortisone to prevent the next faint
nodes.chainStep: Discharge: explain the mechanism and the good prognosis; trigger avoidance; salt and fluids unless contraindicated; counter-pressure maneuvers; driving advice
nodes.why: An uncomplicated faint or situational syncope with nothing else of concern needs no further immediate management. Explain the mechanism, advise on triggers and how to avoid them, and reassure about the good prognosis; promote salt and fluid intake unless contraindicated, and teach counter-pressure maneuvers, which help when the warning lasts long enough. A tilt test is not offered once the history has made the diagnosis, and drugs such as fludrocortisone are for frequent faints: after an occasional one, reassure and teach.

sources.where: Recommendations for vasovagal syncope; treatment strategy; physical counterpressure maneuver

orders.dose: The mechanism, possible triggers and how to avoid them, a good prognosis; see the GP if it recurs or changes
Promote intake unless contraindicated
Useful when the warning period is long enough; they do not work with a minimal or absent prodrome

sources.where: Recommendations, Class IIa; physical counterpressure maneuver

orders.dose: Reduce or withdraw where possible
For frequent faints only; do not treat someone who has not fainted in the past year
Advise on eligibility to drive at this first presentation, under the local licensing rules (NICE points to the UK DVLA)

nodes.summary: Uncomplicated faint: home, with an explanation, trigger advice, salt and fluids, counter-pressure maneuvers and reassurance about the prognosis; no tilt test and no drugs after an occasional faint.

nodes.ask: Postural hypotension, no red flags. Next?
options: Review and reduce the drugs that lower pressure, and explain the cause
Start midodrine and keep every current drug unchanged
Admit for telemetry and an echo to exclude a cardiac cause
Home with an ambulatory ECG to look for an arrhythmia
nodes.chainStep: Review and adjust pressure-lowering drugs such as diuretics; explain the mechanism and what to do if it recurs; standing pressures at follow-up; specialist care if symptoms persist
nodes.why: Postural hypotension sends you to the likely causes, above all the drug list; diuretics are the example the guideline gives. Explain the mechanism, the treatment options and what to do after another blackout, and measure later pressures standing. A firm diagnosis of postural hypotension is an exception to specialist cardiovascular referral, so no admission or ambulatory ECG; specialist care comes only if symptoms persist once the causes are addressed.

orders.dose: Consider likely causes, including current medication; measure later pressures standing
If symptoms persist despite addressing the likely causes
Advise on eligibility to drive at this first presentation, under the local licensing rules (NICE points to the UK DVLA)

nodes.summary: Postural hypotension from a drug: review and reduce the culprit, explain the cause, recheck standing pressures; specialist care only if symptoms persist.

nodes.ask: Unexplained syncope, no red flags, normal ECG and standing pressure. Next?
options: Home with specialist cardiovascular follow-up and an ambulatory ECG
Reassure and discharge with no follow-up, since the ECG is normal
Home with a tilt-table test booked before any ambulatory ECG
An EEG and a neurology referral to look for epilepsy
nodes.chainStep: Discharge with return advice; specialist cardiovascular assessment; ambulatory ECG by event frequency; no driving while waiting; record any further event
nodes.why: Everyone with a blackout goes on to a specialist cardiovascular assessment unless the first assessment made a firm diagnosis of a faint, situational syncope or postural hypotension, or strongly suggested epilepsy. Unexplained syncope gets an ambulatory ECG, never a tilt test before it, and EEG is not routine. A low Canadian Syncope Risk Score supports discharge with clear return advice. The patient must not drive while waiting for the specialist, and a video or a witness account of any further event helps.

orders.dose: For every blackout without a firm diagnosis of faint, situational syncope or postural hypotension, or features strongly suggesting epilepsy
By event frequency; an implantable recorder when events come less often than every 2 weeks
Must not drive while waiting for the specialist assessment
Record them: a video or a detailed witness account

nodes.summary: Unexplained syncope without red flags: home with return advice, specialist cardiovascular assessment and an ambulatory ECG; no driving while waiting.

results.front: Monitor: sustained regular broad-complex tachycardia at 188.

cases.label: A trip, not a blackout

cases.label: Seizure, not syncope
cases.vignette: 26-year-old man, collapsed while sitting on a bus; a witness saw him go stiff, then jerk all four limbs for about two minutes. BP 128/76, HR 104.

results.event: Bitten on the side of the tongue, head turned to one side as he went down, confused for 20 minutes afterward. Glucose 98 mg/dL.

cases.label: Syncope from a GI bleed
cases.vignette: 69-year-old man taking naproxen for knee pain, fainted getting up from the toilet; black stools for 2 days. BP 104/62, HR 112.

results.event: Black tarry stool on rectal exam. Hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL; 14.2 a year ago.

cases.label: Faint with a positive pregnancy test
cases.vignette: 27-year-old woman, fainted at work and has a dull left lower abdominal ache. Last period 7 weeks ago. BP 108/68, HR 104.

results.event: Urine pregnancy test positive. Mild left lower quadrant tenderness, no guarding.

cases.label: Syncope with new breathlessness
cases.vignette: 54-year-old woman, 9 days after a knee replacement, fainted walking to the bathroom and is now short of breath. BP 112/70, HR 118, SpO2 89% on air.

results.event: Breathless at rest, SpO2 89% on air, right calf swollen and tender. Glucose 104 mg/dL.

cases.label: Still in shock after the collapse
cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with hypertension who smokes, collapsed at home with sudden severe back pain. BP 82/50, HR 118.

results.front: Monitor: sinus tachycardia 118. BP 82/50, still hypotensive after coming round; severe back pain, a tender pulsatile mass above the umbilicus.

cases.label: Ischemic ECG after a faint
cases.vignette: 68-year-old woman with diabetes, fainted at the kitchen sink after feeling lightheaded and sweaty; no chest pain. BP 134/80, HR 88.

results.event: Went pale and slumped, came round within a minute, fully oriented. No chest pain, no headache, not breathless. Glucose 142 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL.
results.flags: ECG: new 2 mm ST depression in V4 to V6, not on her ECG from last year.

cases.label: Collapse with tearing chest pain
cases.vignette: 59-year-old man with hypertension, sudden tearing chest pain through to his back, then a brief blackout. BP 168/94, HR 98.

results.event: The pain began seconds before he blacked out and still tears through to his back. Glucose 120 mg/dL. Not breathless.

cases.label: Collapse with a sudden severe headache
cases.vignette: 44-year-old woman, a sudden severe headache while unloading groceries, then a brief collapse; now awake and vomiting. BP 156/92, HR 84.

results.event: The headache reached full strength within seconds, just before she went down; her neck is stiff. Glucose 104 mg/dL. Pregnancy test negative.

cases.label: Mobitz II with syncope, pressure holding
cases.vignette: 76-year-old man, two blackouts this week without warning, the second at the dinner table. Well now. BP 138/80, HR 66.

results.front: Monitor: sinus rhythm, rate 66, an occasional dropped beat. BP 138/80, alert.
results.event: Witnesses: he slumped, went pale and came round within a minute, fully oriented. No tongue bite. Glucose 104 mg/dL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL. Not breathless.
results.flags: ECG: sinus rhythm with dropped beats and no PR lengthening before them (Mobitz II), right bundle branch block.

cases.label: Long QT with syncope
cases.vignette: 23-year-old woman, collapsed when her alarm clock went off this morning; her roommate saw a few seconds of jerking. Takes no medicines. BP 118/74, HR 64.

results.event: Pale and limp, a few seconds of jerking, awake and oriented within a minute; no tongue bite, no confusion after. Glucose 92 mg/dL. Pregnancy test negative.
results.flags: ECG: sinus rhythm, QTc 530 ms. No murmur; no known family history of sudden death.

cases.label: Exertional syncope, aortic stenosis
cases.vignette: 79-year-old man, fainted walking up a hill and came round within a minute. He has tired more easily on hills for months. BP 128/84, HR 76.

results.event: Went down halfway up the hill, came round within a minute, fully alert; no jerking or tongue bite. Glucose 110 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL. Not breathless now.
results.flags: Harsh ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the neck. ECG: sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy.
results.echo_result: Echo: severe calcific aortic stenosis; left ventricle thick-walled, ejection fraction normal.

cases.label: HCM in a young athlete
cases.vignette: 19-year-old college basketball player, collapsed during a sprint drill and came round within a minute. BP 122/70, HR 70.

results.event: Collapsed mid-sprint, pale, awake within a minute, no confusion afterward. Glucose 96 mg/dL. Not breathless.
results.flags: Systolic murmur at the left sternal border that gets louder on standing. ECG: deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads.
results.echo_result: Echo: asymmetric septal hypertrophy, septum 24 mm, resting outflow gradient 60 mm Hg with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.

cases.label: Family history of sudden death, normal echo
cases.vignette: 34-year-old woman, fainted while sitting on the sofa and came round within a minute. Her father died suddenly at 38. BP 120/76, HR 72.

results.event: Slumped and went pale, came round within a minute, fully oriented. No tongue bite. Glucose 94 mg/dL. Pregnancy test negative. Not breathless.
results.flags: No murmur, no heart failure. ECG: sinus rhythm, normal intervals, no Brugada pattern or pre-excitation. Her father died suddenly at 38 with no cause found.
results.echo_result: Echo: structurally normal heart, normal function.

cases.label: Over 65, no warning
cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman, sudden blackout while seated in church with no warning; she slid off the pew. Well now. BP 142/82, HR 70.

results.event: Slumped without any warning, pale, came round in under a minute and knew where she was. No tongue bite. Glucose 118 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL. Not breathless.
results.flags: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, normal intervals. No murmur, no heart failure, no family history of sudden death; no warning at all before the blackout.

cases.label: Uncomplicated faint
cases.vignette: 21-year-old woman, fainted while having blood taken: felt hot, sweaty and sick, then went down; came round within seconds. Her first faint. BP 116/72, HR 68.

results.event: Pale, a few brief twitches, awake within 30 seconds and fully oriented. No tongue bite. Glucose 90 mg/dL. Pregnancy test negative.
results.flags: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, normal intervals. No murmur, no exertion, no family history of sudden death.
results.type: Lying 116/72; standing 112/74 at 1 and 3 minutes. A clear trigger (the needle), with sweating and warmth beforehand. Canadian Syncope Risk Score -3: vasovagal predisposition -1, ED diagnosis of vasovagal syncope -2.

cases.label: Postural hypotension on a new diuretic
cases.vignette: 79-year-old man started on hydrochlorothiazide 3 weeks ago, fainted standing up quickly from the dinner table after a week of dizziness on standing. BP 146/84, HR 76.

results.event: Went lightheaded as he stood, then slumped; came round within a minute, fully oriented. Glucose 108 mg/dL, hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL. Not breathless.
results.flags: ECG: sinus rhythm, normal intervals. No murmur, no heart failure, no family history of sudden death.
results.type: Lying 148/84; standing 118/72 at 1 minute and 116/70 at 3 minutes, with the same lightheadedness.

cases.label: Unexplained syncope, low risk
cases.vignette: 36-year-old man, fainted while sitting at his desk after a few seconds of lightheadedness and came round within a minute. He has fainted twice before when having blood taken. BP 124/78, HR 70.

results.event: Slumped in his chair, pale, came round within a minute, fully oriented. No tongue bite. Glucose 96 mg/dL. Not breathless.
results.flags: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, normal intervals. No murmur, no exertion, no family history of sudden death.
results.type: Lying 124/78; standing 122/80 at 1 and 3 minutes. No trigger, no prolonged standing, no typical warning this time. Canadian Syncope Risk Score -1: vasovagal predisposition -1; no ED diagnosis of vasovagal or cardiac syncope; troponin not done, scored 0.
